newsitem.title: USA: AT&T chairman endorses possible Baby Bell merger.
newsitem.headline: AT&T chairman endorses possible Baby Bell merger.

text.p: Far from setting back competition in local phone markets, the merger of AT&T Corp. and a Baby Bell company would act as a spur to increase customer choice, AT&T Chairman Robert Allen said Tuesday.
"Nobody knows the difference between 'competitive' and 'non-competitive' better than AT&T," Allen said in a speech in Boston, adding for emphasis that, "Many of us are reformed monopolists."
However, the top AT&T executive stopped short of commenting on reports that his company is in talks to merge with one of the larger Baby Bells, SBC Communications Inc.

To date, neither AT&T or SBC have commented on whether they are holding talks to merge. Such a deal, if consumated, would create a mega-carrier with a market value of $110 billion, making it the largest corporate merger in history.
Sources familiar with discussions between the two companies have confirmed that merger talks are under way but said a deal is not imminent.

AT&T is the nation's largest long-distance company, serving more than 80 million residential customers and 10 million businesses. SBC dominates local phone service in a seven-state area stretching from Texas to California.
Critics have argued that a combination between AT&T and a Baby Bell would create an insurmountable barrier to competition in the Baby Bell's local phone service region.

Allen responded that such mergers should only be approved if they can act as a spur to greater competition. Global competition and rapid technology changes have altered the rules of the game, he said.

"The combination of long-distance companies and regional operating companies should only be allowed to happen if people have a real choice for local service from real competitors in the regional companies' territories," he said.

Allen argued that even a company with AT&T's financial strength and customer base cannot afford to build local phone networks quickly around the country, delaying its ability to compete with Baby Bells in local markets on an equal footing.

The AT&T chairman said the advantages of combining with a Baby Bell would include the expanded financial capital to invest in local service facilities around the United States. He also said the deal would give AT&T the scale necessary to compete in the emerging world of international mega-carriers.

AT&T has been left waiting at the altar in recent years as MCI Communications Corp. and British Telecommunications Plc agreed to merge in a deal that would create a company valued at nearly $70 billion. That merger awaits U.S. regulatory approval.
France Telecom and Deutsche Telekom, the national phone carriers in France and Germany, each hold 10 percent stakes in Sprint Corp., another leading U.S. long-distance carrier.

Two other Baby Bells, Bell Atlantic Corp. and Nynex Corp. have agreed to merge in a deal that would create the nation's largest provider of local phone services, dominating a region stretching from Maine to Virginia.
